lines.text: Old kingdoms on a great lake, the source of the Nile, years of terror and the hard road since. This is the story of Uganda.
It begins with water. Lake Victoria, Africa's largest lake, formed some four hundred thousand years ago, and from it flows the White Nile.
On its northern shore, in the fifteenth century, the kingdom of Buganda grew strong, and gave the whole country its name.
In 1837 Mutesa the First was born. As king of Buganda he would welcome the first European visitors to his court.
One of them, John Speke, named Lake Victoria as the source of the Nile in 1858. The river leaves the lake at Jinja.
In 1882 the palace at Kasubi was built, and it became the resting place of Buganda's kings.
In the 1880s missionaries made converts at court, and the new king turned on them. The Christians he put to death are remembered as the Uganda Martyrs.
In 1894 Britain declared a protectorate, and for nearly seventy years Uganda was ruled from London.
In 1925 Idi Amin was born. He would rise through the army and seize the country by force.
Milton Obote was born the same year. He would lead Uganda to independence as its first prime minister.
Yoweri Museveni, born in 1944, would take power in 1986, and still holds it today.
In October 1962 Uganda became independent, a young nation on the shores of the great lake.
But in 1971 Amin overthrew Obote. The next year he expelled Uganda's Asian community, tens of thousands of people, given just three months to leave.
In 1976 a hijacked plane landed at Entebbe, and Israeli commandos flew in by night to rescue the hostages.
Two years later Amin invaded Tanzania. Tanzania struck back, and in 1979 its army and Ugandan exiles drove him out.
In the early eighties a new disease appeared. Uganda was among the first countries hit by AIDS, and among the first to fight it openly and cut infections.
In 1987 Joseph Kony's Lord's Resistance Army took up arms, and for years it terrorised the north.
In 1991 the Bwindi forest became a national park. About half the world's mountain gorillas live there.
Joshua Cheptegei, born in 1996, would win Olympic gold over ten thousand metres, to the pride of a nation.
And in 2023 Uganda passed a law with some of the harshest penalties in the world for same-sex relations.
From the shores of Lake Victoria to today, Uganda's story is one of kingdoms, sorrow and resilience.
